corrected_row: | DOC-A.1-181 | **SPECIAL-NAMES paragraph — allowable locale-names and literal values of the LOCALE clause**, §12.3.7 GR5 (§12.3.7.4), optional (documented if provided) | **Provided (2002 and later).** `LOCALE locale-name-1 IS {external-locale-name-1 or literal-4}` accepts the SAME set of identifications in both forms: a **locale tag** — any BCP-47 tag of a CLDR locale or of a culture .NET recognizes (`fr-FR`, `de-CH`, `sr-Latn-RS`, `zh-Hant`), a `-u-` extension allowed — or the root locale spelled `INVARIANT`, `ROOT`, `C`, `POSIX` or `und`. A **POSIX spelling** `ll_CC[.codeset][@modifier]` is normalized before use (`LocaleIdentification.Normalize`): underscores become hyphens, a `.codeset` suffix is ignored (the repertoire is always UTF-16), an `@modifier` that names a CLDR collation type becomes the `-u-co-<type>` extension (`de_DE@phonebook` is `de-DE-u-co-phonebook`), and any other modifier leaves a tag that names no locale. So `fr_FR`, `fr-FR`, `"fr_FR.UTF-8"` and `"fr-FR"` identify the same locale; the comparison is case-insensitive. The word form is limited to what a COBOL word can spell (no `.` or `@`), so `.codeset` and `@modifier` spellings need the literal form. literal-4 shall be an alphanumeric or national literal, not a figurative constant and not zero-length (`COBOLNET0898`); a locale-name declared twice is `COBOLNET1665`. **Availability is decided at RUN time, never at compile time**: any spelling compiles, and a locale that is not available (`LocaleIdentification.IsAvailable` — the root, a locale with CLDR collation data, a site `.tailor` file, or a culture .NET recognizes) raises `EC-LOCALE-MISSING` at the statement that uses it when that check is enabled; with the check not enabled the statement proceeds with the root locale's conventions (a `LOCALE-DATE` through an unavailable `"zz_QQ"` or `"fr_FR@euro"` formats as `09/24/2026`, exactly as `INVARIANT` does). Before 2002 the clause is rejected (`COBOLNET0900`). | `unit:LocaleStateTests.ExternalIdentification_IsNormalized_PerDeterminationL1`; `unit:LocaleStateTests.Availability_IsTheOneKnownLocaleRule`; `conformance:2002/pb64t1_locale_declare` |

IN` a STANDARD-1/-2 alphabet accepts ordinals 1 through 128 (129 or more is `COBOLNET1670`), and ordinal 66 is `A`. The collating sequence is the native order of those characters. Native characters above U+007F have no counterpart in the standard set: they are not members for a class condition `IS alphabet-name` (`é` is not), and no ordinal reaches them. For `CODE-SET` the correspondence converts as the identity — a record of IRV characters is written to and read from the medium unchanged. ⚠ A record character above U+007F under a STANDARD-1, STANDARD-2 or `ASCII` CODE-SET is at present NOT screened: it reaches the medium as its native code unit (`é` is written as X'E9', status 00), where the `EBCDIC` code-set refuses an unrepresentable character; this is an open defect (kb/Work PB-new, CODE-SET identity arm), so a program shall not rely on writing such a character. corrected_row: | DOC-A.1-186 | **SPECIAL-NAMES paragraph, ALPHABET clause, literal phrase — ordinal number of the characters not specified**, §12.3.7 GR7 k) 4. (§12.3.7.4), required + documented (the scheme, not each character) | **The ordinal number of every character is its position in the alphabet's collating sequence, counting the first position as 1, and the unspecified characters are numbered in the order GR7 k) 3. collates them.** A literal-phrase alphabet's coded character set contains every native character — 65,536 UTF-16 code units, for an alphanumeric and a national alphabet alike (`CodedCharacterSet.OrdinalCount`). The characters the literal phrase specifies take ordinals 1 through *n*, one per collating position in the order written (a THROUGH range fills successive positions; an ALSO group shares one position, and that ordinal names its first character, per GR7 k) 6.). The characters NOT specified then take ordinals *n*+1, *n*+2, … in ascending native code order, skipping the specified ones (`CodedCharacterSet.CharAt`). Worked example: `ALPHABET AL IS "Z" "Y" ALSO "W" "X"` has *n* = 3, so ordinal 1 is `Z`, 2 is `Y`, 3 is `X`, 4 is U+0000, 5 is U+0001, and ordinal 70 is `B` (U+0042, the 67th unspecified character). These are the ordinals `SYMBOLIC CHARACTERS … IN alphabet-name` and a numeric `CLASS … IN alphabet-name` literal use. Because an ALSO character has no ordinal of its own, the highest ordinal is 65,536 minus the number of ALSO characters (in the example, ordinal 65,535 is U+FFFF and 65,536 is `COBOLNET1670`). The same in every edition. | — |

corrected_row: | DOC-A.1-198 | **System-names — rules for the formation of a system-name**, §8.3.2.3 (§8.3.2.3.1), optional (documented if provided) | **Provided — one restriction.** A system-name is formed as any COBOL word of the target edition — letters, digits, hyphen, and (2002 and later) underscore, not beginning or ending with a hyphen or underscore (`ABC-` is a syntax error), at most 30 characters (COBOL-85), 31 (2002 and 2014) or 63 (2023), the length limit being `COBOLNET1567` — with ONE added restriction: a system-name shall not consist of digits only, because such a character-string is always read as an integer literal (`OBJECT-COMPUTER. 12345.` is a syntax error, `COBOL0001`). Unlike a user-defined word, a system-name need not contain a letter otherwise: `123ABC`, `MY_BOX-9` and `1-2` are all accepted as computer-names. Which system-names are RECOGNIZED is a separate matter: device-names, switch-names and feature-names are a fixed list (items 189–191; an unknown one is `COBOLNET2241`), code-names are items 183–184, and external-locale-names are item 181. | — |

corrected_record.notes: Optional item PROVIDED (one restriction), not 'not provided': §8.3.2.3.1 lets the implementor add restrictions to COBOL-word formation, and an all-digit system-name - a legal COBOL word, since §8.3.2.2's 'at least one basic letter' binds user-defined words only - is rejected (the lexer reads it as an integer literal). cite.py --check 8.3.2.3.1 'The implementor may define rules for the formation of a system-name that add restrictions to the rules for formation of a COBOL word' -> OK. Probes refute-probe/p198: sn3.cob OBJECT-COMPUTER. 12345. -> COBOL0001 unexpected '12345'; d1.cob OBJECT-COMPUTER. 1-2. -> OK (no letter needed); sn.cob 123ABC / MY_BOX-9-... -> OK at 2023; sn4.cob ABC- -> COBOL0001; sn5.cob 31/32 chars -> COBOLNET1567 limit 30 at 85, 31 at 2002/2014; sn2.cob 64 chars -> COBOLNET1567 limit 63 at 2023; dv.cob unknown device FOO-DEVICE -> COBOLNET2241. Owning note: kb/Work/PB1534, PB280.

reason: The row said 'Not provided ... adds no restriction' and listed 'at least one letter' as a COBOL-word rule. Both wrong: §8.3.2.1 imposes no letter requirement on a COBOL word (§8.3.2.2's 'at least one basic letter' is for user-defined words only), and the compiler rejects an all-digit system-name (OBJECT-COMPUTER. 12345. -> COBOL0001) while accepting a letterless '1-2' (refute-probe/p198/d1.cob). That digits-only rejection is exactly an implementor restriction §8.3.2.3.1 permits, so the item is PROVIDED and must be documented. Also 'item 189 and its neighbours' made precise as items 189-191. Length limits, underscore gate, trailing hyphen and COBOLNET2241 re-probed and correct.
